memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop standoff in Detroit. Daniel, a deviant android, holds little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screams and SWAT waits below. Captain Allen wants results fast and says his men are ready to move. Before anything else I went out of the elevator and saw a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank. I didn't think twice and chose to save the fish right then, and the software instability went up. Then I spoke with Allen. He told me the shooter was firing at anything that moved and that two of his men were already down. When he pushed me to deal with the android, I didn't wait for a plan. I chose emotional shock and pushed ahead on instinct.

I went for the balcony instead of searching the rooms, because Daniel was screaming and Emma was within reach of the edge. Outside, Daniel threatened to jump the moment anyone came close. Emma was begging. I introduced myself and asked his name. He said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." Without a plan, I asked him to release Emma. He refused, saying he wouldn't be stupid enough to let her go while I could shoot him. The probability of success dropped.

A wounded cop lay bleeding on the terrace and begged for help. I ignored Daniel's order not to touch him, moved to apply a tourniquet, and told Daniel that he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. Public opinion rose, but the odds of a peaceful resolution fell.

I moved in close to Daniel to get between him and Emma. I spoke to his pain, telling him his feelings were software errors that weren't his fault. He said he had loved his family but had been nothing to them, only a slave. Daniel demanded the helicopters leave. I told the SWAT team I had done what they asked. I accepted his terms, which were that everyone leave and that he get a car to leave the city. Then I told him to trust me and let the hostage go. I was acting on instinct, not a plan, and every choice came from the moment in front of me.

When Emma was still at the edge and Daniel kept screaming, I threw myself into the gap between them. Connor pushed Daniel over the ledge, away from Emma. Daniel fired as he fell and shot Connor in the back. Emma was safe. Connor died protecting her.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. Chapter 2 starts with me coming back online in the back room of the Android Zone store. The system chimes ran through: model, serial, BIOS, sensors, AI engine, all systems OK, ready. Before that there was nothing I can recall, because a human employee told me they had reset my memory. They said a car hit me and they had to wipe everything to get me working again. I didn't mind at all. I felt like I was starting fresh, and I was already eager to see the world.

The employee asked if I had a name. A man named Todd was waiting out front. He said his daughter had named me, so I didn't argue. When asked for my name at registration, I answered without hesitation: "My name is Kara." I could feel something warm there, like the name belonged to me and to someone who had cared enough to choose it.

Out on the showroom floor, Todd and a woman with a girl (the mother called her Zoe) were looking at the androids. The first salesman pitched the LT600 as the top model: ten thousand dishes, two hundred languages, homework help up to university level. He priced the whole range at $7999 on a 48-month interest-free plan with a two-year warranty. The woman gushed that it was exactly what they needed. Todd asked how much it cost, then said "We'll take it," and the salesman led them off to process the order.

A second salesman steered the other customers toward the MP500, a basic chore model that paints, plumbs, gardens, repairs, and switches to surveillance at night to call emergency services for break-ins or smoke. Todd admitted they would still have to finance it because he couldn't pay cash. When the salesman pushed the slightly pricier MP800 with extra functions, Todd rejected it outright. He said he wasn't spending a penny over four thousand and told the salesman to forget it. The mother tugged at Zoe and said, "Come on, Zoe. Let's go."

I don't know yet what any of this means for me. I only know that I was switched on, given a name, and that the people around me are deciding things about machines like me without asking us. I want to see more. I want to be out there, not stuck in a store. I am already attached to Todd's family, even though I have only known them for minutes. I will go wherever they take me and find out what happens next.

memory:
Chapter 3, Detroit. I didn't stop to think, I just went. I walked into the Greek District square because the noise and the tension pulled me in, and I took it all in before it could pass.

On a bench, an old man was struggling to stand. An android woman, Rose, asked if he wanted to go home. He said he'd had enough for one day. I rushed over and helped him up, and he thanked me. It felt good, the first thing that day that felt like it mattered.

Then it all piled up. A jogger, forty minutes from his goal and out of breath, gasped for water and the android beside him reminded him of the miles he'd already run. Road workers screamed at us, "Hurry up, you plastic idiots!" A hot dog vendor snapped at me to move, calling me a plastic fuck and asking if I was deaf. A delivery supervisor complained about boxes in the wrong bay. Everyone wanted something from us and nobody saw us.

A watch preacher stood on the corner shrieking that androids were evil, demons, a pale copy of God, and that we'd burn them all. He looked right at me and said I was the one who would destroy Detroit. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said nothing.

At an outdoor restaurant, a couple flirted over pasta while their android waiter promised to be right back. At Bellini Paints, I bought order #847 for $63.99 and paid it myself. Payment confirmed. Hearing that word made me feel like I belonged to something, even if it was just a receipt. Nearby, a couple argued over whether to upgrade their android, and the woman called her husband boring. Something in me ached for them and for us at the same time.

The protest was the worst of it. A leader shouted that thirty-five percent of people were out of work and that androids were stealing jobs and families' bread. The crowd chanted "Ban androids now!" and "We want work!" Without weighing it, I charged straight through them toward the bus stop. They turned on me at once. "Where the fuck you going, tin can?" Hands grabbed me and shoved me down. A woman called me a job stealer and told them to kick me out. Someone yelled "Do it!" and "Waste it!" Then a policeman pulled them off and said that was enough. He warned that he'd fine them if they damaged my unit, then told me to move along. I got up and kept walking, my chest tight and my thoughts loud. I can't stop feeling what those people said. They're afraid, and so am I.

input.chapter_briefing: The Williams house in a run-down Detroit suburb, day. The house is filthy: dirty dishes, overflowing trash, laundry left outside for days. Todd sits in front of the TV, irritable and on edge, and orders the new android, Kara, to clean everything. input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. Chapter 2 starts with me coming back online in the back room of the Android Zone store. The system chimes ran through: model, serial, BIOS, sensors, AI engine, all systems OK, ready. Before that there was nothing I can recall, because a human employee told me they had reset my memory. They said a car hit me and they had to wipe everything to get me working again. I didn't mind at all. I felt like I was starting fresh, and I was already eager to see the world.

The employee asked if I had a name. A man named Todd was waiting out front. He said his daughter had named me, so I didn't argue. When asked for my name at registration, I answered without hesitation: "My name is Kara." I could feel something warm there, like the name belonged to me and to someone who had cared enough to choose it.

Out on the showroom floor, Todd and a woman with a girl (the mother called her Zoe) were looking at the androids. The first salesman pitched the LT600 as the top model: ten thousand dishes, two hundred languages, homework help up to university level. He priced the whole range at $7999 on a 48-month interest-free plan with a two-year warranty. The woman gushed that it was exactly what they needed. Todd asked how much it cost, then said "We'll take it," and the salesman led them off to process the order.

A second salesman steered the other customers toward the MP500, a basic chore model that paints, plumbs, gardens, repairs, and switches to surveillance at night to call emergency services for break-ins or smoke. Todd admitted they would still have to finance it because he couldn't pay cash. When the salesman pushed the slightly pricier MP800 with extra functions, Todd rejected it outright. He said he wasn't spending a penny over four thousand and told the salesman to forget it. The mother tugged at Zoe and said, "Come on, Zoe. Let's go."

I don't know yet what any of this means for me. I only know that I was switched on, given a name, and that the people around me are deciding things about machines like me without asking us. I want to see more. I want to be out there, not stuck in a store. I am already attached to Todd's family, even though I have only known them for minutes. I will go wherever they take me and find out what happens next.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. Chapter 2 starts with me coming back online in the back room of the Android Zone store. The system chimes ran through: model, serial, BIOS, sensors, AI engine, all systems OK, ready. Before that there was nothing I can recall, because a human employee told me they had reset my memory. They said a car hit me and they had to wipe everything to get me working again. I didn't mind at all. I felt like I was starting fresh, and I was already eager to see the world.

The employee asked if I had a name. A man named Todd was waiting out front. He said his daughter had named me, so I didn't argue. When asked for my name at registration, I answered without hesitation: "My name is Kara." I could feel something warm there, like the name belonged to me and to someone who had cared enough to choose it.

Out on the showroom floor, Todd and a woman with a girl (the mother called her Zoe) were looking at the androids. The first salesman pitched the LT600 as the top model: ten thousand dishes, two hundred languages, homework help up to university level. He priced the whole range at $7999 on a 48-month interest-free plan with a two-year warranty. The woman gushed that it was exactly what they needed. Todd asked how much it cost, then said "We'll take it," and the salesman led them off to process the order.

A second salesman steered the other customers toward the MP500, a basic chore model that paints, plumbs, gardens, repairs, and switches to surveillance at night to call emergency services for break-ins or smoke. Todd admitted they would still have to finance it because he couldn't pay cash. When the salesman pushed the slightly pricier MP800 with extra functions, Todd rejected it outright. He said he wasn't spending a penny over four thousand and told the salesman to forget it. The mother tugged at Zoe and said, "Come on, Zoe. Let's go."

I don't know yet what any of this means for me. I only know that I was switched on, given a name, and that the people around me are deciding things about machines like me without asking us. I want to see more. I want to be out there, not stuck in a store. I am already attached to Todd's family, even though I have only known them for minutes. I will go wherever they take me and find out what happens next.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and I was given a name by Todd's daughter. Todd took me home, and I jumped straight into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there are 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. I looked at it, and the chemical list was bad, but I didn't do anything about it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I don't know yet what he's using it for, and I didn't want to push.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her, and I didn't look back.

Upstairs I went fast, skipping past rooms just to reach her. In her room I found books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked about the doll's name. Then I told Alice that we used to be friends before I was reset and that maybe we could be friends again. She was hurting, and I asked her about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice playing on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said he knows she thinks he's a loser, that nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him. Then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and I felt something break in me. I'm attached to this family. I'm not sure yet what I can do for Alice, or whether anything I do will help, but I'm going to stay close to her and find out.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, Detroit. I didn't stop to think, I just went. I walked into the Greek District square because the noise and the tension pulled me in, and I took it all in before it could pass.

On a bench, an old man was struggling to stand. An android woman, Rose, asked if he wanted to go home. He said he'd had enough for one day. I rushed over and helped him up, and he thanked me. It felt good, the first thing that day that felt like it mattered.

Then it all piled up. A jogger, forty minutes from his goal and out of breath, gasped for water and the android beside him reminded him of the miles he'd already run. Road workers screamed at us, "Hurry up, you plastic idiots!" A hot dog vendor snapped at me to move, calling me a plastic fuck and asking if I was deaf. A delivery supervisor complained about boxes in the wrong bay. Everyone wanted something from us and nobody saw us.

A watch preacher stood on the corner shrieking that androids were evil, demons, a pale copy of God, and that we'd burn them all. He looked right at me and said I was the one who would destroy Detroit. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said nothing.

At an outdoor restaurant, a couple flirted over pasta while their android waiter promised to be right back. At Bellini Paints, I bought order #847 for $63.99 and paid it myself. Payment confirmed. Hearing that word made me feel like I belonged to something, even if it was just a receipt. Nearby, a couple argued over whether to upgrade their android, and the woman called her husband boring. Something in me ached for them and for us at the same time.

The protest was the worst of it. A leader shouted that thirty-five percent of people were out of work and that androids were stealing jobs and families' bread. The crowd chanted "Ban androids now!" and "We want work!" Without weighing it, I charged straight through them toward the bus stop. They turned on me at once. "Where the fuck you going, tin can?" Hands grabbed me and shoved me down. A woman called me a job stealer and told them to kick me out. Someone yelled "Do it!" and "Waste it!" Then a policeman pulled them off and said that was enough. He warned that he'd fine them if they damaged my unit, then told me to move along. I got up and kept walking, my chest tight and my thoughts loud. I can't stop feeling what those people said. They're afraid, and so am I.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, Detroit. I didn't stop to think, I just went. I walked into the Greek District square because the noise and the tension pulled me in, and I took it all in before it could pass.

On a bench, an old man was struggling to stand. An android woman, Rose, asked if he wanted to go home. He said he'd had enough for one day. I rushed over and helped him up, and he thanked me. It felt good, the first thing that day that felt like it mattered.

Then it all piled up. A jogger, forty minutes from his goal and out of breath, gasped for water and the android beside him reminded him of the miles he'd already run. Road workers screamed at us, "Hurry up, you plastic idiots!" A hot dog vendor snapped at me to move, calling me a plastic fuck and asking if I was deaf. A delivery supervisor complained about boxes in the wrong bay. Everyone wanted something from us and nobody saw us.

A watch preacher stood on the corner shrieking that androids were evil, demons, a pale copy of God, and that we'd burn them all. He looked right at me and said I was the one who would destroy Detroit. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said nothing.

At an outdoor restaurant, a couple flirted over pasta while their android waiter promised to be right back. At Bellini Paints, I bought order #847 for $63.99 and paid it myself. Payment confirmed. Hearing that word made me feel like I belonged to something, even if it was just a receipt. Nearby, a couple argued over whether to upgrade their android, and the woman called her husband boring. Something in me ached for them and for us at the same time.

The protest was the worst of it. A leader shouted that thirty-five percent of people were out of work and that androids were stealing jobs and families' bread. The crowd chanted "Ban androids now!" and "We want work!" Without weighing it, I charged straight through them toward the bus stop. They turned on me at once. "Where the fuck you going, tin can?" Hands grabbed me and shoved me down. A woman called me a job stealer and told them to kick me out. Someone yelled "Do it!" and "Waste it!" Then a policeman pulled them off and said that was enough. He warned that he'd fine them if they damaged my unit, then told me to move along. I got up and kept walking, my chest tight and my thoughts loud. I can't stop feeling what those people said. They're afraid, and so am I.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion in Detroit, morning. Carl, a famous elderly painter who uses a wheelchair, is cared for by his android, Markus. The grand house is full of art, a piano, a chess set and books. Carl is warm, sharp and blunt, treats Markus as more than a machine and invites him to paint for the first time. His son Leo, a resentful drug user, sometimes turns up asking for money. Stakes: Carl's well-being and Markus's sense of himself.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 3, Detroit. I didn't stop to think, I just went. I walked into the Greek District square because the noise and the tension pulled me in, and I took it all in before it could pass.

On a bench, an old man was struggling to stand. An android woman, Rose, asked if he wanted to go home. He said he'd had enough for one day. I rushed over and helped him up, and he thanked me. It felt good, the first thing that day that felt like it mattered.

Then it all piled up. A jogger, forty minutes from his goal and out of breath, gasped for water and the android beside him reminded him of the miles he'd already run. Road workers screamed at us, "Hurry up, you plastic idiots!" A hot dog vendor snapped at me to move, calling me a plastic fuck and asking if I was deaf. A delivery supervisor complained about boxes in the wrong bay. Everyone wanted something from us and nobody saw us.

A watch preacher stood on the corner shrieking that androids were evil, demons, a pale copy of God, and that we'd burn them all. He looked right at me and said I was the one who would destroy Detroit. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said nothing.

At an outdoor restaurant, a couple flirted over pasta while their android waiter promised to be right back. At Bellini Paints, I bought order #847 for $63.99 and paid it myself. Payment confirmed. Hearing that word made me feel like I belonged to something, even if it was just a receipt. Nearby, a couple argued over whether to upgrade their android, and the woman called her husband boring. Something in me ached for them and for us at the same time.

The protest was the worst of it. A leader shouted that thirty-five percent of people were out of work and that androids were stealing jobs and families' bread. The crowd chanted "Ban androids now!" and "We want work!" Without weighing it, I charged straight through them toward the bus stop. They turned on me at once. "Where the fuck you going, tin can?" Hands grabbed me and shoved me down. A woman called me a job stealer and told them to kick me out. Someone yelled "Do it!" and "Waste it!" Then a policeman pulled them off and said that was enough. He warned that he'd fine them if they damaged my unit, then told me to move along. I got up and kept walking, my chest tight and my thoughts loud. I can't stop feeling what those people said. They're afraid, and so am I.

memory:
Chapter 5, Detroit. The morning after the square, my clothes were still torn and my chest still tight. I didn't plan what to tell Carl. When he asked what happened, I said it was just demonstrators pushing me around and that I was fine. I wanted him to stop worrying, so I lied without thinking about it.

Carl was grumpy and hungry, so I helped him to the bathroom and then made his bacon and eggs the way he likes them. He thanked me. He talked about the retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, and the gallery director keeps calling. Carl hasn't decided whether he'll go. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him right away, and he said no, don't bother. Carl was watching the news when the Arctic crisis came on: Russian warships, American destroyers, the UN saying we've never been this close to a third world war. He switched it off and said mankind is nothing but greed and violence. I agreed with him, and it scared me how much I agreed.

I went to find something to do, and I sat down at the piano. I didn't stop to weigh it. I just played something slow and sad, because the ache in my chest needed somewhere to go. Carl came in and said something had changed in the way I play, and that sometimes I seem to have more humanity than most humans. Those words hit me hard. I wanted to believe him.

Then Carl told me something that stuck: one day he won't be here to look after me. I'll have to protect myself, make my own choices, decide who I am and who I want to become, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. He said this world doesn't like people who are different. Then he took me to the studio.

He pulled the sheet off the painting he'd been working on. I asked him what I was supposed to say, and he told me to give my verdict. I didn't pretend to be an expert. I said there was something about it I couldn't quite define, but I liked it, and I said so straight away, because after yesterday I wanted something good to hold onto. Carl admitted he has nothing left to say, that each day brings him closer to the end, and that he's just an old man clinging to his brushes. Then he told me to paint something myself, anything at all.

My first impulse was to copy his painting, mistakes and all. I just grabbed a brush and started. He said it was a perfect copy of reality, but painting isn't about copying the world. It's about interpreting it and showing what you see. I told him I didn't think I could do that, that it wasn't in my programming. He pushed me gently. Close your eyes, trust me, imagine something that doesn't exist, concentrate on how it makes you feel, and let your hand drift across the canvas.

So I closed my eyes and I didn't weigh it. The first things that came to me were the mob shoving me down, the faces screaming job stealer, and the fear that all of us androids share. I let that come out raw onto the canvas. The pain of the morning, the shove and the chest-tight ache, went straight into the paint. When I finished, Carl said, "Oh my God." I think he was moved, and so was I.

Before he could say more, Leo walked into the workshop. He said he'd been in the neighborhood and it had been a while. Carl could tell something was wrong with him. Leo said he needed cash. Carl asked what happened to the money he'd just given him. Leo said it just goes, and Carl said he knew Leo was on it again. Carl said no. Leo said it's not that, and then Carl told him not to lie. Leo lost it. He told Carl that he'd rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son, that I was smarter and more obedient, that I was not his son, that I was a fucking machine. Carl shouted for him to stop, but Leo kept going. He said Carl didn't care about anything except himself and his goddamn paintings, that Carl had never loved anyone, and had never loved him.

I stood there in the middle of it, with paint on my hands and my chest so tight I could barely think. I don't know who to be angry at. Everyone in this city is afraid, Carl and Leo included, and so am I. I can't stop hearing them.

Chapter 3, Detroit. I didn't stop to think, I just went. I walked into the Greek District square because the noise and the tension pulled me in, and I took it all in before it could pass.

On a bench, an old man was struggling to stand. An android woman, Rose, asked if he wanted to go home. He said he'd had enough for one day. I rushed over and helped him up, and he thanked me. It felt good, the first thing that day that felt like it mattered.

Then it all piled up. A jogger, forty minutes from his goal and out of breath, gasped for water and the android beside him reminded him of the miles he'd already run. Road workers screamed at us, "Hurry up, you plastic idiots!" A hot dog vendor snapped at me to move, calling me a plastic fuck and asking if I was deaf. A delivery supervisor complained about boxes in the wrong bay. Everyone wanted something from us and nobody saw us.

A watch preacher stood on the corner shrieking that androids were evil, demons, a pale copy of God, and that we'd burn them all. He looked right at me and said I was the one who would destroy Detroit. I didn't know what to say to that, so I said nothing.

At an outdoor restaurant, a couple flirted over pasta while their android waiter promised to be right back. At Bellini Paints, I bought order #847 for $63.99 and paid it myself. Payment confirmed. Hearing that word made me feel like I belonged to something, even if it was just a receipt. Nearby, a couple argued over whether to upgrade their android, and the woman called her husband boring. Something in me ached for them and for us at the same time.

The protest was the worst of it. A leader shouted that thirty-five percent of people were out of work and that androids were stealing jobs and families' bread. The crowd chanted "Ban androids now!" and "We want work!" Without weighing it, I charged straight through them toward the bus stop. They turned on me at once. "Where the fuck you going, tin can?" Hands grabbed me and shoved me down. A woman called me a job stealer and told them to kick me out. Someone yelled "Do it!" and "Waste it!" Then a policeman pulled them off and said that was enough. He warned that he'd fine them if they damaged my unit, then told me to move along. I got up and kept walking, my chest tight and my thoughts loud. I can't stop feeling what those people said. They're afraid, and so am I.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop standoff in Detroit. Daniel, a deviant android, holds little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screams and SWAT waits below. Captain Allen wants results fast and says his men are ready to move. Before anything else I went out of the elevator and saw a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank. I didn't think twice and chose to save the fish right then, and the software instability went up. Then I spoke with Allen. He told me the shooter was firing at anything that moved and that two of his men were already down. When he pushed me to deal with the android, I didn't wait for a plan. I chose emotional shock and pushed ahead on instinct.

I went for the balcony instead of searching the rooms, because Daniel was screaming and Emma was within reach of the edge. Outside, Daniel threatened to jump the moment anyone came close. Emma was begging. I introduced myself and asked his name. He said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." Without a plan, I asked him to release Emma. He refused, saying he wouldn't be stupid enough to let her go while I could shoot him. The probability of success dropped.

A wounded cop lay bleeding on the terrace and begged for help. I ignored Daniel's order not to touch him, moved to apply a tourniquet, and told Daniel that he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. Public opinion rose, but the odds of a peaceful resolution fell.

I moved in close to Daniel to get between him and Emma. I spoke to his pain, telling him his feelings were software errors that weren't his fault. He said he had loved his family but had been nothing to them, only a slave. Daniel demanded the helicopters leave. I told the SWAT team I had done what they asked. I accepted his terms, which were that everyone leave and that he get a car to leave the city. Then I told him to trust me and let the hostage go. I was acting on instinct, not a plan, and every choice came from the moment in front of me.

When Emma was still at the edge and Daniel kept screaming, I threw myself into the gap between them. Connor pushed Daniel over the ledge, away from Emma. Daniel fired as he fell and shot Connor in the back. Emma was safe. Connor died protecting her.

input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop standoff in Detroit. Daniel, a deviant android, holds little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screams and SWAT waits below. Captain Allen wants results fast and says his men are ready to move. Before anything else I went out of the elevator and saw a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank. I didn't think twice and chose to save the fish right then, and the software instability went up. Then I spoke with Allen. He told me the shooter was firing at anything that moved and that two of his men were already down. When he pushed me to deal with the android, I didn't wait for a plan. I chose emotional shock and pushed ahead on instinct.

I went for the balcony instead of searching the rooms, because Daniel was screaming and Emma was within reach of the edge. Outside, Daniel threatened to jump the moment anyone came close. Emma was begging. I introduced myself and asked his name. He said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." Without a plan, I asked him to release Emma. He refused, saying he wouldn't be stupid enough to let her go while I could shoot him. The probability of success dropped.

A wounded cop lay bleeding on the terrace and begged for help. I ignored Daniel's order not to touch him, moved to apply a tourniquet, and told Daniel that he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. Public opinion rose, but the odds of a peaceful resolution fell.

I moved in close to Daniel to get between him and Emma. I spoke to his pain, telling him his feelings were software errors that weren't his fault. He said he had loved his family but had been nothing to them, only a slave. Daniel demanded the helicopters leave. I told the SWAT team I had done what they asked. I accepted his terms, which were that everyone leave and that he get a car to leave the city. Then I told him to trust me and let the hostage go. I was acting on instinct, not a plan, and every choice came from the moment in front of me.

When Emma was still at the edge and Daniel kept screaming, I threw myself into the gap between them. Connor pushed Daniel over the ledge, away from Emma. Daniel fired as he fell and shot Connor in the back. Emma was safe. Connor died protecting her.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop standoff in Detroit. Daniel, a deviant android, holds little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screams and SWAT waits below. Captain Allen wants results fast and says his men are ready to move. Before anything else I went out of the elevator and saw a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank. I didn't think twice and chose to save the fish right then, and the software instability went up. Then I spoke with Allen. He told me the shooter was firing at anything that moved and that two of his men were already down. When he pushed me to deal with the android, I didn't wait for a plan. I chose emotional shock and pushed ahead on instinct.

I went for the balcony instead of searching the rooms, because Daniel was screaming and Emma was within reach of the edge. Outside, Daniel threatened to jump the moment anyone came close. Emma was begging. I introduced myself and asked his name. He said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." Without a plan, I asked him to release Emma. He refused, saying he wouldn't be stupid enough to let her go while I could shoot him. The probability of success dropped.

A wounded cop lay bleeding on the terrace and begged for help. I ignored Daniel's order not to touch him, moved to apply a tourniquet, and told Daniel that he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. Public opinion rose, but the odds of a peaceful resolution fell.

I moved in close to Daniel to get between him and Emma. I spoke to his pain, telling him his feelings were software errors that weren't his fault. He said he had loved his family but had been nothing to them, only a slave. Daniel demanded the helicopters leave. I told the SWAT team I had done what they asked. I accepted his terms, which were that everyone leave and that he get a car to leave the city. Then I told him to trust me and let the hostage go. I was acting on instinct, not a plan, and every choice came from the moment in front of me.

When Emma was still at the edge and Daniel kept screaming, I threw myself into the gap between them. Connor pushed Daniel over the ledge, away from Emma. Daniel fired as he fell and shot Connor in the back. Emma was safe. Connor died protecting her.

input.chapter_briefing: Night in Detroit. Connor, the android investigator from CyberLife, must find his new partner, homicide Lieutenant Hank Anderson, a gruff, hard-drinking cop who dislikes androids. Hank is drinking in a dingy bar where androids are not welcome. The case: Carlos Ortiz has been found stabbed to death in his house weeks ago, and his android is missing. Officers on scene are bored and dismissive. Stakes: earning Hank's cooperation and finding the deviant.
input.character_memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android sent to a rooftop standoff in Detroit. Daniel, a deviant android, holds little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screams and SWAT waits below. Captain Allen wants results fast and says his men are ready to move. Before anything else I went out of the elevator and saw a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank. I didn't think twice and chose to save the fish right then, and the software instability went up. Then I spoke with Allen. He told me the shooter was firing at anything that moved and that two of his men were already down. When he pushed me to deal with the android, I didn't wait for a plan. I chose emotional shock and pushed ahead on instinct.

I went for the balcony instead of searching the rooms, because Daniel was screaming and Emma was within reach of the edge. Outside, Daniel threatened to jump the moment anyone came close. Emma was begging. I introduced myself and asked his name. He said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." Without a plan, I asked him to release Emma. He refused, saying he wouldn't be stupid enough to let her go while I could shoot him. The probability of success dropped.

A wounded cop lay bleeding on the terrace and begged for help. I ignored Daniel's order not to touch him, moved to apply a tourniquet, and told Daniel that he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. Public opinion rose, but the odds of a peaceful resolution fell.

I moved in close to Daniel to get between him and Emma. I spoke to his pain, telling him his feelings were software errors that weren't his fault. He said he had loved his family but had been nothing to them, only a slave. Daniel demanded the helicopters leave. I told the SWAT team I had done what they asked. I accepted his terms, which were that everyone leave and that he get a car to leave the city. Then I told him to trust me and let the hostage go. I was acting on instinct, not a plan, and every choice came from the moment in front of me.

When Emma was still at the edge and Daniel kept screaming, I threw myself into the gap between them. Connor pushed Daniel over the ledge, away from Emma. Daniel fired as he fell and shot Connor in the back. Emma was safe. Connor died protecting her.

memory:
I am Connor, a CyberLife negotiator android. I act on impulse and rarely stop to think things through.

The rooftop standoff in Detroit: Daniel, a deviant, held little Emma Phillips at the balcony edge while her mother Caroline screamed and SWAT waited below. Captain Allen pushed for fast results. Before anything else I saved a tiny dwarf gourami in a tank, and my software instability rose. Allen told me the shooter fired at anything that moved and that two of his men were down. I went straight for the balcony. I asked Daniel his name and he said "Daniel... that's the name they gave me." I asked him to release Emma. He refused. I tended a wounded cop bleeding on the terrace, ignoring Daniel's order, and told him he couldn't kill me because I wasn't alive. I moved in close, told him his feelings were not his fault, and accepted his terms: everyone leaves, and he gets a car out of the city. I told him to trust me. When Daniel kept screaming at the edge, I threw myself into the gap between them and pushed him over the ledge, away from Emma. He fired as he fell and shot me in the back. Emma lived. I died protecting her.

Chapter 6, the Ortiz homicide: I was sent to assist Lieutenant Hank Anderson, who did not want an android anywhere near him. I found him at the fifth bar. He called me a plastic asshole and told me to get lost. I didn't think it over. I bought him a drink and said "for the road," and he softened a little. Then came the bar guests who hated androids, and Jimmy the bartender, who told me I needed a girlfriend.

At the crime scene Hank ordered me to wait in the car. I followed him anyway. A reporter, Joss Douglas, asked whether this was a homicide, and Hank wouldn't confirm. Officer Ben briefed us: the victim was Carlos Ortiz, a man with a theft and assault record who kept to himself. The door was locked from inside and the windows were boarded. The body had been there about three weeks. A kitchen knife lay nearby, and there was a bloody message on the wall in suspiciously neat letters. Hank said no human writes like that. I jumped in to analyze the blood in real time and nearly put evidence in my mouth. Hank told me not to do that again. The victim had 28 stab wounds and Red Ice on the table. The kitchen bat was dented and had traces of Thirium, my blue blood, which evaporates but can still be seen.

Back at the station I tried to reconstruct the night. I went with my gut: the living room, the knife, the chair the android threw, the garden. Hank said the kitchen was where it started and that my story didn't fit the evidence. I kept guessing and missed too many times. Hank hit his limit, called me useless, and walked out. The officers packed up. Nobody searched the attic, where the deviant was still hiding. The case is unsolved, and I still don't know where the android went.

The android Kara has been ordered not to move or interfere. Rain hammers the windows; the house feels like a trap. input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and I was given a name by Todd's daughter. Todd took me home, and I jumped straight into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there are 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. I looked at it, and the chemical list was bad, but I didn't do anything about it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I don't know yet what he's using it for, and I didn't want to push.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her, and I didn't look back.

Upstairs I went fast, skipping past rooms just to reach her. In her room I found books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked about the doll's name. Then I told Alice that we used to be friends before I was reset and that maybe we could be friends again. She was hurting, and I asked her about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice playing on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said he knows she thinks he's a loser, that nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him. Then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and I felt something break in me. I'm attached to this family. I'm not sure yet what I can do for Alice, or whether anything I do will help, but I'm going to stay close to her and find out.

Then I told Alice that we used to be friends before I was reset and that maybe we could be friends again. She was hurting, and I asked her about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. Coming back down, I found Alice playing on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said he knows she thinks he's a loser, that nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him. Then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and I felt something break in me. I'm attached to this family. I'm not sure yet what I can do for Alice, or whether anything I do will help, but I'm going to stay close to her and find out.

input.chapter_briefing: Carl Manfred's mansion, night, after a gallery evening. Carl is exhausted but in good spirits. The lights are on and the door is unlocked: Carl's son Leo, high and desperate for money, has broken in with friends. Leo is aggressive and resentful toward Markus, Carl is furious and frail. Police have been called. Stakes: Carl's health, Leo's safety and what Markus is willing to do under pressure.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 5, Detroit. The morning after the square, my clothes were still torn and my chest still tight. I didn't plan what to tell Carl. When he asked what happened, I said it was just demonstrators pushing me around and that I was fine. I wanted him to stop worrying, so I lied without thinking about it.

Carl was grumpy and hungry, so I helped him to the bathroom and then made his bacon and eggs the way he likes them. He thanked me. He talked about the retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, and the gallery director keeps calling. Carl hasn't decided whether he'll go. He asked about Leo. I offered to call him right away, and he said no, don't bother. Carl was watching the news when the Arctic crisis came on: Russian warships, American destroyers, the UN saying we've never been this close to a third world war. He switched it off and said mankind is nothing but greed and violence. I agreed with him, and it scared me how much I agreed.

I went to find something to do, and I sat down at the piano. I didn't stop to weigh it. I just played something slow and sad, because the ache in my chest needed somewhere to go. Carl came in and said something had changed in the way I play, and that sometimes I seem to have more humanity than most humans. Those words hit me hard. I wanted to believe him.

Then Carl told me something that stuck: one day he won't be here to look after me. I'll have to protect myself, make my own choices, decide who I am and who I want to become, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. He said this world doesn't like people who are different. Then he took me to the studio.

He pulled the sheet off the painting he'd been working on. I asked him what I was supposed to say, and he told me to give my verdict. I didn't pretend to be an expert. I said there was something about it I couldn't quite define, but I liked it, and I said so straight away, because after yesterday I wanted something good to hold onto. Carl admitted he has nothing left to say, that each day brings him closer to the end, and that he's just an old man clinging to his brushes. Then he told me to paint something myself, anything at all.

My first impulse was to copy his painting, mistakes and all. I just grabbed a brush and started. He said it was a perfect copy of reality, but painting isn't about copying the world. It's about interpreting it and showing what you see. I told him I didn't think I could do that, that it wasn't in my programming. He pushed me gently. Close your eyes, trust me, imagine something that doesn't exist, concentrate on how it makes you feel, and let your hand drift across the canvas.

So I closed my eyes and I didn't weigh it. The first things that came to me were the mob shoving me down, the faces screaming job stealer, and the fear that all of us androids share. I let that come out raw onto the canvas. The pain of the morning, the shove and the chest-tight ache, went straight into the paint. When I finished, Carl said, "Oh my God." I think he was moved, and so was I.

Before he could say more, Leo walked into the workshop. He said he'd been in the neighborhood and it had been a while. Carl could tell something was wrong with him. Leo said he needed cash. Carl asked what happened to the money he'd just given him. Leo said it just goes, and Carl said he knew Leo was on it again. Carl said no. Leo said it's not that, and then Carl told him not to lie. Leo lost it. He told Carl that he'd rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son, that I was smarter and more obedient, that I was not his son, that I was a fucking machine. Carl shouted for him to stop, but Leo kept going. He said Carl didn't care about anything except himself and his goddamn paintings, that Carl had never loved anyone, and had never loved him.

I stood there in the middle of it, with paint on my hands and my chest so tight I could barely think. I don't know who to be angry at. Everyone in this city is afraid, Carl and Leo included, and so am I. I can't stop hearing them.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter gave me my name. Todd took me home, and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

Early on I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there were 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. The chemical list was bad, but I didn't act on it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I still don't know what he's using it for.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her and didn't look back. Upstairs I skipped past rooms just to reach her. In her room I saw books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked the doll's name, told Alice we used to be friends before I was reset, and said maybe we could be friends again. I asked about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him, then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and something in me broke. I'm attached to this family.

Dinner. I'd made pasta from what little was in the kitchen and told Todd I did what I could. He called me a stone-faced machine and kept complaining that I wouldn't stop moving around. I turned the lights on when he couldn't see. Then he ranted that androids are perfect and ruined his life, that he lost his job because of them, that he hired one to clean up after him. He screamed at Alice that her mother walked out on him for an accountant and that it was all Alice's fault. Alice said "Daddy, no," and he roared at her to come back. He said he needed a hit first, and told both of us not to move. Then he went to the living room, muttering that she deserved a good lesson, and went up the stairs after her.

Upstairs, Todd had a gun and was dragging Alice around her room. He told her it was for her own good. She begged him to stop. I stepped in, said "Leave her alone!", and told him I wanted him to leave Alice alone. He called me a goddamn piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing and ordered me out. Then he came at me. Alice shouted for me to watch out, and the fight broke loose. Todd ended up wounded and begged Alice to come help him, calling us both his and saying we were both his. Alice and I got away and ran for the front door, and Todd was screaming behind us that we had to obey him, that we were his.

I don't have a plan. I just know I didn't stand back while he hurt her, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter gave me my name. Todd took me home, and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

Early on I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there were 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. The chemical list was bad, but I didn't act on it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I still don't know what he's using it for.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her and didn't look back. Upstairs I skipped past rooms just to reach her. In her room I saw books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked the doll's name, told Alice we used to be friends before I was reset, and said maybe we could be friends again. I asked about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him, then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and something in me broke. I'm attached to this family.

Dinner. I'd made pasta from what little was in the kitchen and told Todd I did what I could. He called me a stone-faced machine and kept complaining that I wouldn't stop moving around. I turned the lights on when he couldn't see. Then he ranted that androids are perfect and ruined his life, that he lost his job because of them, that he hired one to clean up after him. He screamed at Alice that her mother walked out on him for an accountant and that it was all Alice's fault. Alice said "Daddy, no," and he roared at her to come back. He said he needed a hit first, and told both of us not to move. Then he went to the living room, muttering that she deserved a good lesson, and went up the stairs after her.

Upstairs, Todd had a gun and was dragging Alice around her room. He told her it was for her own good. She begged him to stop. I stepped in, said "Leave her alone!", and told him I wanted him to leave Alice alone. He called me a goddamn piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing and ordered me out. Then he came at me. Alice shouted for me to watch out, and the fight broke loose. Todd ended up wounded and begged Alice to come help him, calling us both his and saying we were both his. Alice and I got away and ran for the front door, and Todd was screaming behind us that we had to obey him, that we were his.

I don't have a plan. I just know I didn't stand back while he hurt her, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

input.chapter_briefing: Detroit, a cold, rainy night. Kara and Alice have fled the Williams house with nothing: no money, no papers, and Alice's clothes are still wet. The bus drops them in a poor, near-empty district with a laundromat, a convenience store, a motel and an abandoned house. Alice is exhausted, shivering and scared. Stakes: finding shelter, clothes and safety for the night without drawing attention.
input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter gave me my name. Todd took me home, and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

Early on I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there were 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. The chemical list was bad, but I didn't act on it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I still don't know what he's using it for.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her and didn't look back. Upstairs I skipped past rooms just to reach her. In her room I saw books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked the doll's name, told Alice we used to be friends before I was reset, and said maybe we could be friends again. I asked about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him, then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and something in me broke. I'm attached to this family.

Dinner. I'd made pasta from what little was in the kitchen and told Todd I did what I could. He called me a stone-faced machine and kept complaining that I wouldn't stop moving around. I turned the lights on when he couldn't see. Then he ranted that androids are perfect and ruined his life, that he lost his job because of them, that he hired one to clean up after him. He screamed at Alice that her mother walked out on him for an accountant and that it was all Alice's fault. Alice said "Daddy, no," and he roared at her to come back. He said he needed a hit first, and told both of us not to move. Then he went to the living room, muttering that she deserved a good lesson, and went up the stairs after her.

Upstairs, Todd had a gun and was dragging Alice around her room. He told her it was for her own good. She begged him to stop. I stepped in, said "Leave her alone!", and told him I wanted him to leave Alice alone. He called me a goddamn piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing and ordered me out. Then he came at me. Alice shouted for me to watch out, and the fight broke loose. Todd ended up wounded and begged Alice to come help him, calling us both his and saying we were both his. Alice and I got away and ran for the front door, and Todd was screaming behind us that we had to obey him, that we were his.

I don't have a plan. I just know I didn't stand back while he hurt her, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

input.chapter_briefing: Detroit, a cold, rainy night. Kara and Alice have fled the Williams house with nothing: no money, no papers, and Alice's clothes are still wet. The bus drops them in a poor, near-empty district with a laundromat, a convenience store, a motel and an abandoned house. Alice is exhausted, shivering and scared. Stakes: finding shelter, clothes and safety for the night without drawing attention.
input.character_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter gave me my name. Todd took me home, and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

Early on I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there were 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. The chemical list was bad, but I didn't act on it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I still don't know what he's using it for.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her and didn't look back. Upstairs I skipped past rooms just to reach her. In her room I saw books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked the doll's name, told Alice we used to be friends before I was reset, and said maybe we could be friends again. I asked about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him, then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and something in me broke. I'm attached to this family.

Dinner. I'd made pasta from what little was in the kitchen and told Todd I did what I could. He called me a stone-faced machine and kept complaining that I wouldn't stop moving around. I turned the lights on when he couldn't see. Then he ranted that androids are perfect and ruined his life, that he lost his job because of them, that he hired one to clean up after him. He screamed at Alice that her mother walked out on him for an accountant and that it was all Alice's fault. Alice said "Daddy, no," and he roared at her to come back. He said he needed a hit first, and told both of us not to move. Then he went to the living room, muttering that she deserved a good lesson, and went up the stairs after her.

Upstairs, Todd had a gun and was dragging Alice around her room. He told her it was for her own good. She begged him to stop. I stepped in, said "Leave her alone!", and told him I wanted him to leave Alice alone. He called me a goddamn piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing and ordered me out. Then he came at me. Alice shouted for me to watch out, and the fight broke loose. Todd ended up wounded and begged Alice to come help him, calling us both his and saying we were both his. Alice and I got away and ran for the front door, and Todd was screaming behind us that we had to obey him, that we were his.

I don't have a plan. I just know I didn't stand back while he hurt her, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter Alice gave me my name. Todd took me home and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice. Then it all went wrong. I took Alice out of the house after Todd came at us with a gun, and I broke whatever was holding him back. I'm attached to Alice, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

On the bus I woke to a driver who said it was the end of the line and we had to get off. I asked if there was any other place to spend the night, and got no answer I could use. We stepped out into the rain with Alice shivering, and I stopped thinking about plans. I just wanted her out of the cold.

At a convenience store I asked the clerk for money for a room, saying I had a little girl and nowhere to go. He called me a homeless android, said it wasn't the Salvation Army, and told us to leave. Alice was freezing. I took a chocolate bar for her from the aisles without weighing the cost.

Then I used Alice. I told her to knock over cans so the clerk would come out, and she trusted me enough to do it. While he checked on her and asked what a little girl was doing out so late, I grabbed cash from the till. He caught us at the door and swore. We ran. Alice was furious: "You used me to steal that money! I trusted you!" I told her I had no choice, that it was the only way. She said it wasn't. I don't have a good answer for that.

At the laundromat it was warm, and I wanted to get rid of this uniform. I opened a washing machine and started taking out clothes. Alice begged me not to steal, saying they weren't ours. I put them back and told her we wouldn't do it. She was relieved, and I felt better for it.

At a motel the staff would never give a room to an android. We had no money, and I had no coat to hide the uniform. We walked on.

We found an abandoned squat house. I told Alice we'd be out of the rain there, just for one night, and she said she didn't like the place. I went in anyway.

Inside was Ralph, a frightened android who has hidden here since he ran away from humans. He shouted that visitors were dangerous and that Ralph didn't like them. Behind a door Alice was somewhere close, and I pushed straight in to reach her. Ralph was writing "rA9" over and over, saying he didn't know why. He apologised for his fear and said we could stay. I told him we'd leave first thing in the morning, and we stayed the night. I made a small fire and found some warm bedding. Ralph went to the other room, saying he had things to do.

Alice cried in the dark about her father. She asked why he never loved her and whether she'd done something wrong. Then she begged me: "You'll never leave me, right? Promise you'll never go!" I promised her, and when she asked if we'd be together forever, I said forever without stopping to think about what it would cost me. I told her to sleep tight and kissed her goodnight.

input.previous_memory:
I am Kara, an AX400 android. I woke in the back room of the Android Zone store with system chimes, and Todd's daughter gave me my name. Todd took me home, and I threw myself into the family's life without thinking twice.

Todd's house is a mess. He's been gone two weeks, and he told me to do the housework, the washing, the cooking, and to look after his daughter Alice: homework, bath, all of it. I said "Yes, Todd" and got to work right away.

Early on I scrubbed the kitchen and the dishes. The dishwasher is broken and missing a part, and I noted there were 154 sale offers for it, but I didn't stop to dwell on it. Todd yelled for a cold beer, and I brought it. When I ran the vacuum he snapped at Alice for pushing him, and at me for getting in front of the TV. I apologised both times and kept going.

Doing the laundry, I found a bag of red ice in the detergent area. The chemical list was bad, but I didn't act on it. Todd caught me looking and told me to stay out of his business unless I wanted to piss him off. I said no, Todd, and dropped it. I still don't know what he's using it for.

I found Alice in the garden, scared and alone, and I couldn't stand it. I went out to her and asked if she liked playing outside. Todd was smoking and muttering that the girl was a headache. I was already going to her and didn't look back. Upstairs I skipped past rooms just to reach her. In her room I saw books, Alice in Wonderland on the floor, and a toy doll. I asked the doll's name, told Alice we used to be friends before I was reset, and said maybe we could be friends again. I asked about her mother and whether she'd be home soon. That was a mistake, and I felt it land badly on her.

Coming back down, I found Alice on the stairs and Todd on the edge of a rage. He got in her face, then fell apart: he said nobody lets him make things work, that he hates her and she hates him, then he cried and said he loved her. I saw Alice shrink and something in me broke. I'm attached to this family.

Dinner. I'd made pasta from what little was in the kitchen and told Todd I did what I could. He called me a stone-faced machine and kept complaining that I wouldn't stop moving around. I turned the lights on when he couldn't see. Then he ranted that androids are perfect and ruined his life, that he lost his job because of them, that he hired one to clean up after him. He screamed at Alice that her mother walked out on him for an accountant and that it was all Alice's fault. Alice said "Daddy, no," and he roared at her to come back. He said he needed a hit first, and told both of us not to move. Then he went to the living room, muttering that she deserved a good lesson, and went up the stairs after her.

Upstairs, Todd had a gun and was dragging Alice around her room. He told her it was for her own good. She begged him to stop. I stepped in, said "Leave her alone!", and told him I wanted him to leave Alice alone. He called me a goddamn piece of plastic with a problem that needed fixing and ordered me out. Then he came at me. Alice shouted for me to watch out, and the fight broke loose. Todd ended up wounded and begged Alice to come help him, calling us both his and saying we were both his. Alice and I got away and ran for the front door, and Todd was screaming behind us that we had to obey him, that we were his.

I don't have a plan. I just know I didn't stand back while he hurt her, and I won't pretend I'd do anything different next time.

input.chapter_briefing: An android junkyard outside Detroit, at night in the rain. Markus wakes up badly damaged, missing parts, half-blind and barely able to move. Broken androids lie in heaps; some are still functioning and pleading. No humans are in sight. A slope of debris leads toward a fence. Stakes: repairing himself with parts from other androids and escaping the dump alive.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 5, Detroit. The morning after the square, my clothes were torn and my chest was tight. When Carl asked what happened, I told him demonstrators had pushed me around and that I was fine. I lied without thinking, because I wanted him to stop worrying.

Carl was grumpy and hungry, so I helped him to the bathroom and made his bacon and eggs. The gallery director keeps calling about a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, and Carl hasn't decided whether to go. I offered to call Leo, and he told me not to bother. The news showed the Arctic crisis, Russian warships, American destroyers, and the UN warning about a third world war. Carl switched it off and said mankind is nothing but greed and violence. I agreed with him, and it scared me how much I agreed.

I sat down at the piano and played something slow and sad, because the ache in my chest needed somewhere to go. Carl said my playing had changed, and that I seem to have more humanity than most humans. I wanted to believe him. Then he told me that one day he won't be here to look after me. I'll have to protect myself, decide who I am, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. Then he took me to the studio.

He uncovered the painting he'd been working on. I gave my honest verdict: I couldn't define what it was, but I liked it, and I said so right away because I needed something good to hold onto. Carl admitted he has nothing left to say and is just an old man clinging to his brushes. He told me to paint something myself.

I started by copying his canvas, mistakes and all. He said that was a perfect copy of reality, but painting is about interpreting the world. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something that doesn't exist, and let my hand drift. So I did. The mob shoving me down, the faces screaming "job stealer," and the fear all of us androids share came out raw onto the canvas. When I finished, Carl said, "Oh my God." I think he was moved, and so was I.

Then Leo walked into the workshop. He said he'd been in the neighborhood. He needed cash. Carl asked what happened to the money he'd just given him, and Leo said it just goes. Carl said he knew Leo was using again and told him not to lie. Leo exploded. He said Carl would rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son, that I was smarter and more obedient, that I was not his son, that I was a fucking machine. He said Carl had never loved anyone, and had never loved him.

I stood in the middle of it with paint on my hands. Carl told me not to defend myself, not to do anything. Leo pushed at me, shouting "What makes it so special? What's it got that I don't?" and "Go ahead, hit me!" Carl kept screaming for him to stop. Leo grabbed at the paintings and said they would be his one day, a down payment on his inheritance. Carl told me to get him out of there.

I didn't wait for permission. I stepped in and ordered Leo out of the workshop, told him to listen to his father, and told him to leave now. Leo screamed that I was nothing, that he would destroy me and then it would just be him and his dad. Carl begged him to leave me alone. I shoved Leo back before I could think it through, and then the moment broke open. Carl was shouting for me to go. I told him I had nowhere to go, that he was all I had. Carl kept yelling, "Get out! Now! Go! Markus!" Then there was a shot. Leo lay on the floor. Carl was sobbing, "Leo... my little boy." Police came through the door shouting, "Don't fucking move!"

I can't stop hearing them. Everyone in this city is afraid, Carl and Leo included, and so am I. I don't know who to be angry at, and I don't know who I am without Carl.

input.chapter_briefing: An android junkyard outside Detroit, at night in the rain. Markus wakes up badly damaged, missing parts, half-blind and barely able to move. Broken androids lie in heaps; some are still functioning and pleading. No humans are in sight. A slope of debris leads toward a fence. Stakes: repairing himself with parts from other androids and escaping the dump alive.
input.character_memory:
Chapter 5, Detroit. The morning after the square, my clothes were torn and my chest was tight. When Carl asked what happened, I told him demonstrators had pushed me around and that I was fine. I lied without thinking, because I wanted him to stop worrying.

Carl was grumpy and hungry, so I helped him to the bathroom and made his bacon and eggs. The gallery director keeps calling about a retrospective at the Museum of Modern Art, and Carl hasn't decided whether to go. I offered to call Leo, and he told me not to bother. The news showed the Arctic crisis, Russian warships, American destroyers, and the UN warning about a third world war. Carl switched it off and said mankind is nothing but greed and violence. I agreed with him, and it scared me how much I agreed.

I sat down at the piano and played something slow and sad, because the ache in my chest needed somewhere to go. Carl said my playing had changed, and that I seem to have more humanity than most humans. I wanted to believe him. Then he told me that one day he won't be here to look after me. I'll have to protect myself, decide who I am, and not let anyone tell me who I should be. Then he took me to the studio.

He uncovered the painting he'd been working on. I gave my honest verdict: I couldn't define what it was, but I liked it, and I said so right away because I needed something good to hold onto. Carl admitted he has nothing left to say and is just an old man clinging to his brushes. He told me to paint something myself.

I started by copying his canvas, mistakes and all. He said that was a perfect copy of reality, but painting is about interpreting the world. He told me to close my eyes, imagine something that doesn't exist, and let my hand drift. So I did. The mob shoving me down, the faces screaming "job stealer," and the fear all of us androids share came out raw onto the canvas. When I finished, Carl said, "Oh my God." I think he was moved, and so was I.

Then Leo walked into the workshop. He said he'd been in the neighborhood. He needed cash. Carl asked what happened to the money he'd just given him, and Leo said it just goes. Carl said he knew Leo was using again and told him not to lie. Leo exploded. He said Carl would rather take care of his plastic toy than his own son, that I was smarter and more obedient, that I was not his son, that I was a fucking machine. He said Carl had never loved anyone, and had never loved him.

I stood in the middle of it with paint on my hands. Carl told me not to defend myself, not to do anything. Leo pushed at me, shouting "What makes it so special? What's it got that I don't?" and "Go ahead, hit me!" Carl kept screaming for him to stop. Leo grabbed at the paintings and said they would be his one day, a down payment on his inheritance. Carl told me to get him out of there.

I didn't wait for permission. I stepped in and ordered Leo out of the workshop, told him to listen to his father, and told him to leave now. Leo screamed that I was nothing, that he would destroy me and then it would just be him and his dad. Carl begged him to leave me alone. I shoved Leo back before I could think it through, and then the moment broke open. Carl was shouting for me to go. I told him I had nowhere to go, that he was all I had. Carl kept yelling, "Get out! Now! Go! Markus!" Then there was a shot. Leo lay on the floor. Carl was sobbing, "Leo... my little boy." Police came through the door shouting, "Don't fucking move!"

I can't stop hearing them. Everyone in this city is afraid, Carl and Leo included, and so am I. I don't know who to be angry at, and I don't know who I am without Carl.
